**COMPLETE CONTENT** (803 lines):

```rust
//! PURPOSE: The SSRF egress guard — the policy every production outbound
//! HTTP call goes through.
//!
//! Owning layer: `mas-integrations`.
//!
//! Production responsibility: decide whether a destination is reachable at
//! all: reject link-local, loopback, and metadata addresses unless a caller
//! names them explicitly as internal endpoints.
//!
//! Security boundary: without this, any feature that fetches a URL becomes a
//! request forgery into the cluster. Reaching a private range is a decision
//! somebody makes on purpose, in code, for a named host.
//!
//! It must NOT:
//!   • allow a redirect to re-target an approved request into a private
//!     range;
//!   • be optional for production callers — `HttpDispatcher` holds one and
//!     every dispatch goes through it;
//!   • resolve a hostname more than once (DNS rebinding).

//! Hardened egress: the SSRF enforcement layer promised by `SafeUrl`.
//!
//! `SafeUrl` performs first-line validation at parse time (scheme, no
//! embedded credentials, no private/loopback IP literals). This module adds
//! everything parse time *cannot* know:
//!
//! * [`EgressPolicy`] — operator-configured scheme/port/hostname allowlists
//!   plus `pin_resolution`, which a production client MUST call with the
//!   DNS answers and refuse the request when any answer is non-global (the
//!   conservative DNS-rebinding/TOCTOU rule).
//! * [`GuardedHttpClient`] — wraps an [`HttpClientPort`], re-validates
//!   EVERY redirect hop (a redirect to `http://169.254.169.254/…` is a
//!   classic SSRF pivot), applies redirect count and response body caps.
//!
//! The crate deliberately ships no concrete network client; worker/api
//! processes bind a real HTTP stack to [`HttpClientPort`]. A scriptable
//! recorder implementation lives in the tests of this module.

use async_trait::async_trait;
use mas_common::error::AppError;
use mas_common::result::Result;
use mas_domain::value_objects::SafeUrl;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::collections::BTreeSet;
use std::net::{IpAddr, Ipv4Addr};
use url::Url;

/// Default maximum redirect hops a guarded request may follow.
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_REDIRECTS: u8 = 3;
/// Default response body cap (1 MiB).
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_BYTES: usize = 1 << 20;
/// Default per-request timeout budget.
pub const DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS: u64 = 30_000;

/// Operator-configured egress policy.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct EgressPolicy {
    /// Require TLS for every outbound request (default: `true`). Plain
    /// `http` is then allowed only for hosts named in
    /// `permitted_plain_http_hosts`.
    pub https_only: bool,
    /// Exact hostnames (or parent domains) permitted to be reached over
    /// plain HTTP despite `https_only` — dev/test fixtures only.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub permitted_plain_http_hosts: BTreeSet<String>,
    /// Explicit port allowlist. `None` ⇒ only the scheme's default port
    /// (443 for https, 80 for http).
    #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub allowed_ports: Option<BTreeSet<u16>>,
    /// Optional hostname allowlist applied on top of everything else;
    /// exact match or subdomain.
    #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub hostname_allowlist: Option<BTreeSet<String>>,
    pub max_redirects: u8,
    pub max_body_bytes: usize,
    /// Whether URLs parsed as operator-declared internal endpoints
    /// (`SafeUrl::parse_internal_endpoint`) may be contacted.
    ///
    /// Default `false`. When `true`, [`Self::hostname_allowlist`] is
    /// **mandatory**: the exception is granted to a named destination, not to
    /// "anything private".
    ///
    /// This exists because platform services legitimately call each other over
    /// the cluster network. It is not a way to reach a tenant-supplied
    /// private address — a URL from tenant data is never parsed as an internal
    /// endpoint, and the flag on the `SafeUrl` is what distinguishes the two.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub allow_internal_endpoints: bool,
}

impl Default for EgressPolicy {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            https_only: true,
            permitted_plain_http_hosts: BTreeSet::new(),
            allowed_ports: None,
            hostname_allowlist: None,
            max_redirects: DEFAULT_MAX_REDIRECTS,
            max_body_bytes: DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_BYTES,
            allow_internal_endpoints: false,
        }
    }
}

impl EgressPolicy {
    /// A policy for one operator-declared internal service endpoint.
    ///
    /// `hosts` names the exact hosts the platform may reach over the cluster
    /// network — `mas-api`, `127.0.0.1`, a Kubernetes service DNS name. Plain
    /// HTTP is permitted for them because cluster traffic is commonly not TLS
    /// terminated, and every other restriction (redirect re-validation, body
    /// caps, redirect limits) stays in force.
    ///
    /// The allowlist is required: an internal-endpoint policy with no
    /// allowlist would be an open permit to reach any private address, which
    /// is the exact vulnerability the guard exists to prevent.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn for_internal_endpoints<I, S>(hosts: I, allowed_ports: Option<BTreeSet<u16>>) -> Self
    where
        I: IntoIterator<Item = S>,
        S: Into<String>,
    {
        let hosts: BTreeSet<String> = hosts.into_iter().map(Into::into).collect();
        Self {
            https_only: false,
            permitted_plain_http_hosts: hosts.clone(),
            allowed_ports,
            hostname_allowlist: Some(hosts),
            max_redirects: DEFAULT_MAX_REDIRECTS,
            max_body_bytes: DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_BYTES,
            allow_internal_endpoints: true,
        }
    }
}

impl EgressPolicy {
    /// Validates that `url` may be contacted under this policy.
    ///
    /// `SafeUrl` guarantees parse-level safety; this layer applies the
    /// operator policy on scheme, port and hostname.
    pub fn check_destination(&self, url: &SafeUrl) -> Result<()> {
        // An internal endpoint is permitted only when the policy opted in, and
        // then only if it also passes the hostname allowlist below. A URL that
        // merely *claims* to be internal cannot get through a policy that never
        // enabled them.
        if url.is_internal_endpoint() {
            if !self.allow_internal_endpoints {
                return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                    "url",
                    "internal_endpoint_forbidden",
                    "this egress policy does not permit internal endpoints",
                ));
            }
            if self.hostname_allowlist.is_none() {
                return Err(AppError::internal(
                    "internal endpoints are enabled without a hostname allowlist; \
                     refusing to contact anything",
                ));
            }
        }

        let parsed = Url::parse(url.as_str()).map_err(|err| {
            AppError::internal(format!("validated SafeUrl failed re-parse: {err}"))
        })?;
        let host = parsed.host_str().unwrap_or_default().to_ascii_lowercase();

        match parsed.scheme() {
            "https" => {},
            "http" => {
                let permitted = !self.https_only
                    || self
                        .permitted_plain_http_hosts
                        .iter()
                        .any(|allowed| host == *allowed || host.ends_with(&format!(".{allowed}")));
                if !permitted {
                    return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                        "url",
                        "plain_http_forbidden",
                        format!("plain HTTP to '{host}' is not permitted by the egress policy"),
                    ));
                }
            },
            scheme => {
                return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                    "url",
                    "invalid_scheme",
                    format!("scheme '{scheme}' is not allowed (http/https only)"),
                ));
            },
        }

        let port = parsed.port_or_known_default().ok_or_else(|| {
            AppError::invalid_field("url", "missing_port", "no port could be determined")
        })?;
        match &self.allowed_ports {
            Some(set) if !set.contains(&port) => {
                return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                    "url",
                    "forbidden_port",
                    format!("port {port} is not in the egress allowlist"),
                ));
            },
            Some(_) => {},
            None => {
                let default_port = url.is_tls();
                let expected = if default_port { 443 } else { 80 };
                if port != expected {
                    return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                        "url",
                        "forbidden_port",
                        format!(
                            "port {port} is not the scheme default without an explicit allowlist"
                        ),
                    ));
                }
            },
        }

        if let Some(allowlist) = &self.hostname_allowlist {
            let allowed = allowlist
                .iter()
                .any(|entry| host == *entry || host.ends_with(&format!(".{entry}")));
            if !allowed {
                return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                    "url",
                    "host_not_allowlisted",
                    format!("host '{host}' is not in the egress hostname allowlist"),
                ));
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    /// DNS-resolution gate (anti-rebinding). The real HTTP client resolves
    /// the hostname, calls this with every answer, and connects ONLY to the
    /// returned address. Conservative rule: if ANY answer is non-global,
    /// the whole request is refused — a hostile DNS record must not smuggle
    /// a private address past us among good ones.
    pub fn pin_resolution(&self, resolved: &[IpAddr]) -> Result<IpAddr> {
        self.pin_resolution_public(resolved)
    }

    /// Resolution gate for a destination that may legitimately be private.
    ///
    /// `internal_endpoint` comes from the URL and is honoured only when the
    /// policy allows internal endpoints at all. For an internal endpoint the
    /// requirement relaxes from "publicly routable" to "not a link-local or
    /// metadata address": reaching `10.0.0.5` is the point, but reaching
    /// `169.254.169.254` never is, not even from inside the cluster.
    pub fn pin_resolution_for(
        &self,
        resolved: &[IpAddr],
        internal_endpoint: bool,
    ) -> Result<IpAddr> {
        if internal_endpoint && self.allow_internal_endpoints {
            for addr in resolved {
                if is_metadata_or_link_local(addr) {
                    return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                        "url",
                        "forbidden_host",
                        format!("destination resolves to metadata/link-local address {addr}"),
                    ));
                }
            }
            return Ok(resolved[0]);
        }
        self.pin_resolution_public(resolved)
    }

    /// The public-only resolution gate.
    fn pin_resolution_public(&self, resolved: &[IpAddr]) -> Result<IpAddr> {
        if resolved.is_empty() {
            return Err(AppError::external_service(
                "http-egress",
                "destination resolved to no addresses",
            ));
        }
        for addr in resolved {
            if !is_publicly_routable(addr) {
                return Err(AppError::invalid_field(
                    "url",
                    "forbidden_host",
                    format!("destination resolves to non-public address {addr}"),
                ));
            }
        }
        Ok(resolved[0])
    }
}

/// Whether an address is a link-local or cloud-metadata address.
///
/// Never reachable, not even from an operator-declared internal endpoint:
/// `169.254.0.0/16` is the metadata service on every major cloud, and a
/// platform service calling its own API has no business being able to read
/// instance credentials.
#[must_use]
pub fn is_metadata_or_link_local(addr: &IpAddr) -> bool {
    match addr {
        IpAddr::V4(ip) => ip.is_link_local() || ip.is_unspecified() || ip.is_broadcast(),
        IpAddr::V6(ip) => {
            if let Some(mapped) = ip.to_ipv4_mapped() {
                return mapped.is_link_local() || mapped.is_unspecified() || mapped.is_broadcast();
            }
            ip.is_unspecified() || (ip.segments()[0] & 0xffc0) == 0xfe80
        },
    }
}

/// Whether an address is safe to connect to from the platform. Complements
/// `SafeUrl`'s literal-time checks with full IPv6 ranges: unique-local
/// (`fc00::/7`), link-local (`fe80::/10`) and IPv4-mapped addresses are
/// classified via their embedded IPv4 rules.
#[must_use]
pub fn is_publicly_routable(addr: &IpAddr) -> bool {
    match addr {
        IpAddr::V4(ip) => ipv4_is_public(ip),
        IpAddr::V6(ip) => {
            if let Some(mapped) = ip.to_ipv4_mapped() {
                return ipv4_is_public(&mapped);
            }
            !(ip.is_loopback()
                || ip.is_unspecified()
                || ip.is_multicast()
                || (ip.segments()[0] & 0xfe00) == 0xfc00 // fc00::/7 unique-local
                || (ip.segments()[0] & 0xffc0) == 0xfe80) // fe80::/10 link-local
        },
    }
}

fn ipv4_is_public(ip: &Ipv4Addr) -> bool {
    !(ip.is_loopback()
        || ip.is_private()
        || ip.is_link_local()
        || ip.is_unspecified()
        || ip.is_broadcast()
        || ip.is_documentation()
        || ip.is_multicast()
        || ip.octets()[0] == 0
        // CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10
        || (ip.octets()[0] == 100 && (ip.octets()[1] & 0xC0) == 64)
        // benchmarking 198.18.0.0/15
        || (ip.octets()[0] == 198 && (ip.octets()[1] == 18 || ip.octets()[1] == 19))
        // reserved + broadcast space 240.0.0.0/4
        || ip.octets()[0] >= 240)
}

/// HTTP method supported by the egress plane.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum HttpMethod {
    /// `GET`.
    Get,
    /// `POST`.
    Post,
    /// `PUT`.
    Put,
}

impl HttpMethod {
    /// Canonical wire token.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn as_token(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Get => "GET",
            Self::Post => "POST",
            Self::Put => "PUT",
        }
    }
}

/// A validated outbound request.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct HttpRequest {
    pub method: HttpMethod,
    pub url: SafeUrl,
    /// Lowercased header names; credential headers are only ever attached
    /// by callers, never echoed in errors.
    pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
    pub body: Vec<u8>,
    pub timeout_ms: u64,
}

impl HttpRequest {
    /// A bare GET.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn get(url: SafeUrl) -> Self {
        Self {
            method: HttpMethod::Get,
            url,
            headers: Vec::new(),
            body: Vec::new(),
            timeout_ms: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS,
        }
    }

    /// A POST with a body.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn post(url: SafeUrl, body: Vec<u8>) -> Self {
        Self {
            method: HttpMethod::Post,
            url,
            headers: Vec::new(),
            body,
            timeout_ms: DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS,
        }
    }

    /// Builder: set a header (name lowercased).
    #[must_use]
    pub fn with_header(mut self, name: &str, value: &str) -> Self {
        self.headers
            .push((name.to_ascii_lowercase(), value.to_owned()));
        self
    }

    /// Builder: override the timeout budget.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn with_timeout_ms(mut self, timeout_ms: u64) -> Self {
        self.timeout_ms = timeout_ms;
        self
    }
}

/// A received response (already size-capped by the guard).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct HttpResponse {
    pub status: u16,
    /// Header names are lowercased.
    pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
    pub body: Vec<u8>,
}

impl HttpResponse {
    /// Synthetic response for tests/fakes.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn new(status: u16) -> Self {
        Self {
            status,
            headers: Vec::new(),
            body: Vec::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Whether the status is 2xx.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn is_success(&self) -> bool {
        self.status >= 200 && self.status < 300
    }

    /// Whether the status is a redirect.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn is_redirect(&self) -> bool {
        matches!(self.status, 301 | 302 | 303 | 307 | 308)
    }

    /// Case-insensitive header lookup.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn header(&self, name: &str) -> Option<&str> {
        let wanted = name.to_ascii_lowercase();
        self.headers
            .iter()
            .find(|(key, _)| *key == wanted)
            .map(|(_, value)| value.as_str())
    }

    /// Parsed `Retry-After` seconds, when present and well-formed.
    /// HTTP-date form is intentionally unsupported by the egress plane;
    /// callers fall back to their own backoff.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn retry_after_seconds(&self) -> Option<u64> {
        self.header("retry-after")?.trim().parse().ok()
    }
}

/// The outbound HTTP port real clients bind to.
#[async_trait]
pub trait HttpClientPort: std::fmt::Debug + Send + Sync {
    /// Sends a pre-validated request. Implementations MUST enforce
    /// `request.timeout_ms`, resolve DNS through
    /// [`EgressPolicy::pin_resolution`], and cap reads at
    /// `EgressPolicy::max_body_bytes`.
    async fn send(&self, request: &HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse>;
}

/// Policy-enforcing wrapper around an [`HttpClientPort`].
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct GuardedHttpClient<S: HttpClientPort> {
    inner: S,
    policy: EgressPolicy,
}

impl<S: HttpClientPort> GuardedHttpClient<S> {
    /// Wraps `inner` under `policy`.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn new(inner: S, policy: EgressPolicy) -> Self {
        Self { inner, policy }
    }

    /// The active egress policy.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn policy(&self) -> &EgressPolicy {
        &self.policy
    }

    /// The wrapped client.
    #[must_use]
    pub const fn inner(&self) -> &S {
        &self.inner
    }

    /// Sends `request`, enforcing:
    /// 1. destination policy (scheme/port/host),
    /// 2. redirect re-validation of EVERY `Location` hop (relative or
    ///    absolute), 303 → GET with an empty body,
    /// 3. redirect and body caps.
    pub async fn send(&self, request: &HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse> {
        let mut current = request.clone();
        let mut hops: u8 = 0;
        loop {
            self.policy.check_destination(&current.url)?;
            let response = self.inner.send(&current).await.map_err(|err| {
                err.with_context(format!("egress call to {} failed", current.url.host_str()))
            })?;

            if !(response.is_redirect() && response.header("location").is_some()) {
                if response.body.len() > self.policy.max_body_bytes {
                    return Err(AppError::external_service(
                        "http-egress",
                        format!(
                            "response body exceeded the {} byte cap",
                            self.policy.max_body_bytes
                        ),
                    ));
                }
                return Ok(response);
            }

            hops += 1;
            if hops > self.policy.max_redirects {
                return Err(AppError::external_service(
                    "http-egress",
                    format!(
                        "redirect limit of {} hops exceeded",
                        self.policy.max_redirects
                    ),
                ));
            }
            let location = response.header("location").unwrap_or_default();
            let base = Url::parse(current.url.as_str()).map_err(|err| {
                AppError::internal(format!("validated SafeUrl failed re-parse: {err}"))
            })?;
            let joined = base.join(location).map_err(|err| {
                AppError::external_service(
                    "http-egress",
                    format!("invalid redirect location: {err}"),
                )
            })?;
            let next_url = SafeUrl::parse(joined.as_str())?;
            if response.status == 303 {
                current.method = HttpMethod::Get;
                current.body.clear();
            }
            current.url = next_url;
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use std::net::Ipv6Addr;
    use std::sync::Mutex;

    fn safe(raw: &str) -> SafeUrl {
        SafeUrl::parse(raw).expect("safe url")
    }

    #[test]
    fn policy_enforces_scheme_port_and_allowlist() {
        let policy = EgressPolicy::default();
        assert!(policy
            .check_destination(&safe("https://api.example.com/x"))
            .is_ok());
        assert!(
            policy
                .check_destination(&safe("http://api.example.com/x"))
                .is_err(),
            "https_only default"
        );
        assert!(
            policy
                .check_destination(&safe("https://api.example.com:8443/x"))
                .is_err(),
            "non-default port blocked"
        );

        let mut dev = EgressPolicy::default();
        dev.permitted_plain_http_hosts
            .insert("local.test".to_owned());
        assert!(dev
            .check_destination(&safe("http://api.local.test/x"))
            .is_ok());

        let ported = EgressPolicy {
            allowed_ports: Some(BTreeSet::from([8443_u16])),
            ..EgressPolicy::default()
        };
        assert!(ported
            .check_destination(&safe("https://api.example.com:8443/x"))
            .is_ok());
        assert!(
            ported
                .check_destination(&safe("https://api.example.com/x"))
                .is_err(),
            "443 not in port allowlist"
        );

        let scoped = EgressPolicy {
            hostname_allowlist: Some(BTreeSet::from(["example.com".to_owned()])),
            ..EgressPolicy::default()
        };
        assert!(scoped
            .check_destination(&safe("https://api.example.com/x"))
            .is_ok());
        assert!(scoped
            .check_destination(&safe("https://attacker.io/x"))
            .is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    fn resolution_pinning_rejects_non_global_and_accepts_public() {
        let policy = EgressPolicy::default();
        assert!(policy.pin_resolution(&[]).is_err());
        assert!(policy
            .pin_resolution(&[IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(93, 184, 216, 34))])
            .is_ok());
        assert!(
            policy
                .pin_resolution(&[
                    IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(93, 184, 216, 34)),
                    IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(10, 0, 0, 7)),
                ])
                .is_err(),
            " ONE private answer poisons the whole set"
        );
        assert!(policy
            .pin_resolution(&[IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(127, 0, 0, 1))])
            .is_err());
        assert!(
            policy
                .pin_resolution(&[IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(169, 254, 169, 254))])
                .is_err(),
            "cloud metadata"
        );
        assert!(
            policy
                .pin_resolution(&[IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(100, 64, 0, 1))])
                .is_err(),
            "CGNAT"
        );
        let mapped: Ipv6Addr = "::ffff:192.168.1.5".parse().expect("v6 literal");
        assert!(
            !is_publicly_routable(&IpAddr::V6(mapped)),
            "v4-mapped falls back to v4 rules"
        );
        let ula: Ipv6Addr = "fd00::1".parse().expect("v6 literal");
        assert!(!is_publicly_routable(&IpAddr::V6(ula)), "unique-local");
        let link: Ipv6Addr = "fe80::1".parse().expect("v6 literal");
        assert!(!is_publicly_routable(&IpAddr::V6(link)), "link-local");
        let global: Ipv6Addr = "2606:4700:4700::1111".parse().expect("v6 literal");
        assert!(is_publicly_routable(&IpAddr::V6(global)));
    }

    /// Scriptable recorder client used by guard and webhook tests alike?
    /// (webhook tests define their own; this one serves the guard tests).
    #[derive(Debug, Default)]
    struct ScriptClient {
        recorded: Mutex<Vec<HttpRequest>>,
        routes: Mutex<Vec<(SafeUrl, HttpResponse)>>,
    }

    impl ScriptClient {
        fn route(&self, url: &str, response: HttpResponse) {
            self.routes
                .lock()
                .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
                .push((safe(url), response));
        }
    }

    #[async_trait]
    impl HttpClientPort for ScriptClient {
        async fn send(&self, request: &HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse> {
            self.recorded
                .lock()
                .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
                .push(request.clone());
            let mut routes = self.routes.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
            if let Some(position) = routes
                .iter()
                .position(|(u, _)| u.as_str() == request.url.as_str())
            {
                return Ok(routes.remove(position).1);
            }
            drop(routes);
            Ok(HttpResponse::new(200))
        }
    }

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn redirect_hops_are_revalidated() {
        let client = ScriptClient::default();
        let mut to_private = HttpResponse::new(302);
        to_private.headers.push((
            "location".to_owned(),
            "http://169.254.169.254/latest".to_owned(),
        ));
        client.route("https://hook.example.test/a", to_private);

        let guarded = GuardedHttpClient::new(client, EgressPolicy::default());
        let result = guarded
            .send(&HttpRequest::post(
                safe("https://hook.example.test/a"),
                vec![1],
            ))
            .await;
        assert!(result.is_err(), "redirect to link-local must be refused");
        // 169.254.169.254 fails `SafeUrl::parse` (link-local literal), so the
        // hop is refused before any second request is sent.
        let sent = guarded
            .inner()
            .recorded
            .lock()
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
            .len();
        assert_eq!(sent, 1, "no request was sent to the redirect target");
    }

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn redirect_follows_allowed_hops_and_caps_bodies() {
        let client = ScriptClient::default();
        let mut bounce = HttpResponse::new(302);
        bounce.headers.push((
            "location".to_owned(),
            "https://final.example.test/ok".to_owned(),
        ));
        client.route("https://hook.example.test/a", bounce);

        let guarded = GuardedHttpClient::new(client, EgressPolicy::default());
        let response = guarded
            .send(&HttpRequest::post(
                safe("https://hook.example.test/a"),
                vec![1, 2, 3],
            ))
            .await
            .expect("valid chain allowed");
        assert_eq!(response.status, 200);
        assert_eq!(
            guarded
                .inner()
                .recorded
                .lock()
                .unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
                .len(),
            2
        );

        // Body cap
        let heavy = ScriptClient::default();
        let mut big = HttpResponse::new(200);
        big.body = vec![0u8; 64];
        heavy.route("https://big.example.test/", big);
        let tiny = EgressPolicy {
            max_body_bytes: 8,
            ..EgressPolicy::default()
        };
        let guarded_tiny = GuardedHttpClient::new(heavy, tiny);
        assert!(guarded_tiny
            .send(&HttpRequest::get(safe("https://big.example.test/")))
            .await
            .is_err());

        // Redirect loop — routes are consumed on use, so seed enough copies
        // to sustain the circle past the hop limit.
        let looped = ScriptClient::default();
        for _ in 0..8 {
            let mut again = HttpResponse::new(302);
            again.headers.push((
                "location".to_owned(),
                "https://loop.example.test/spin".to_owned(),
            ));
            looped.route("https://loop.example.test/spin", again);
        }
        let guarded_loop = GuardedHttpClient::new(looped, EgressPolicy::default());
        assert!(
            guarded_loop
                .send(&HttpRequest::get(safe("https://loop.example.test/spin")))
                .await
                .is_err(),
            "never-ending redirects die at the hop limit"
        );
    }
}

```

## FILE: repo/enterprise-mas/rust-core/migrations/0015_directory_role/up.sql


**PURPOSE:**

```text
The tenancy-directory database role (security Phase 3 / 14).

Owning layer: the database, applied by the migration runner.

Production responsibility: create `mas_directory` -- the one role permitted
to resolve a tenant from identity BEFORE a scope exists -- with BYPASSRLS
confined to SELECT on four catalog tables, and make it NOLOGIN until
provisioning grants it a login. `mas_app` deliberately receives no
BYPASSRLS.

Security boundary: resolving tenancy is a chicken-and-egg read: the
directory must be queried before any GUC can be set, and under
`FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` an unscoped read returns nothing. Rather than
weaken the policies or grant `mas_app` a bypass, this migration creates a
separate, table-confined role and gives the process a separate pool for it.

It must NOT:
• grant BYPASSRLS to `mas_app`;
• grant `mas_directory` anything beyond SELECT on the four catalog
tables;
• let the runtime pool be used for directory reads.

Migration 0015 — the tenancy directory role.

WHY THIS EXISTS (security Phase 3 / 14)
=======================================
Every tenant-owned table is `ENABLE` + `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. The
directory tables that describe the hierarchy (`organizations`, `tenants`,
`projects`, `memberships`) are no exception: a `tenants` row is visible
only when `app.current_tenant` or `app.current_org` already matches it.

That creates a bootstrap that cannot be resolved inside a scoped
transaction. To resolve *which* tenant a request is entitled to, the
platform must first read the hierarchy — but reading the hierarchy already
requires knowing the tenant. Any attempt to solve this inside `mas_app`
would require either (a) granting `mas_app` BYPASSRLS, which would disable
row-level security for every tenant table in the system, or (b) a
`SECURITY DEFINER` function that accepts a user id from the caller, which
would let any caller impersonate any user because SQL has no notion of the
application-level principal. Both are worse than the problem.

The resolution is to confine the exception instead of widening the rule.
This migration creates a dedicated role that:

* exists for exactly one purpose — reading the hierarchy catalog;
* is granted SELECT on the four directory tables and nothing else;
* is granted NO privilege on any tenant data table (executions, tasks,
agents, credentials, usage, audit, outbox, …), so a compromise of this
role discloses the shape of the tenancy tree and no tenant data;
* holds BYPASSRLS, which is unavoidable for a pre-scope read and is the
reason the grant surface above is deliberately minimal.

The application connects to PostgreSQL with TWO pools:

* `mas_app`      — runtime role, NO BYPASSRLS, used for all tenant data.
Every transaction sets `app.current_tenant` /
`app.current_org` with `SET LOCAL` before touching a
row.
* `mas_directory` — this role, used only to resolve a principal's tenant,
organization and project before a scope exists.

INVARIANTS
* `mas_directory` must never be the role behind a request-serving
repository. It has no grants on tenant tables, so an attempt fails
closed at the database, but the code must not rely on that alone.
* `mas_directory` must never receive INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on anything.
* Adding a tenant data table must NOT widen this role's grants; the grant
list below is intentionally explicit rather than `ON ALL TABLES`.

MIGRATION PATH (Phase 14, operational)
1. Apply this migration with the *migrator* role (the schema owner).
2. Create OS-level credentials for `mas_directory` in the secret manager
and grant `mas_directory` login with that password. The role is created
NOLOGIN so an unconfigured deployment cannot accidentally authenticate
as it.
3. Configure `MAS_DATABASE_DIRECTORY_URL` alongside `MAS_DATABASE_URL`.
If it is unset, the API refuses to serve tenant-scoped routes rather
than silently falling back to the runtime role — a fallback to
`mas_app` would mean unscoped directory reads that return zero rows,
which looks like "tenant not found" rather than a misconfiguration.
4. Rotation: create the new credential, update the secret, reload. The
role itself needs no change.
```

--   * holds BYPASSRLS, which is unavoidable for a pre-scope read and is the

--
-- The application connects to PostgreSQL with TWO pools:
--
--   * `mas_app`      — runtime role, NO BYPASSRLS, used for all tenant data.
--                      Every transaction sets `app.current_tenant` /
--                      `app.current_org` with `SET LOCAL` before touching a
--                      row.
--   * `mas_directory` — this role, used only to resolve a principal's tenant,
--                      organization and project before a scope exists.
--
-- INVARIANTS
--   * `mas_directory` must never be the role behind a request-serving
--     repository. It has no grants on tenant tables, so an attempt fails
--     closed at the database, but the code must not rely on that alone.
--   * `mas_directory` must never receive INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on anything.
--   * Adding a tenant data table must NOT widen this role's grants; the grant
--     list below is intentionally explicit rather than `ON ALL TABLES`.
--
-- MIGRATION PATH (Phase 14, operational)
--   1. Apply this migration with the *migrator* role (the schema owner).
--   2. Create OS-level credentials for `mas_directory` in the secret manager
--      and grant `mas_directory` login with that password. The role is created
--      NOLOGIN so an unconfigured deployment cannot accidentally authenticate
--      as it.

--      than silently falling back to the runtime role — a fallback to

BEGIN
    IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'mas_directory') THEN

## FILE: repo/enterprise-mas/rust-core/migrations/0018_api_key_owner/up.sql


**PURPOSE:**

```text
Add the owning-user column that `api_keys` projections already read.

Owning layer: the database, applied by the migration runner.

Production responsibility: create `api_keys.user_id`. The repository
(`crates/persistence/src/repositories/api_keys.rs`) projects `user_id` in
its `COLUMNS` list and reads it in `row_from`, and the API-key use-case
records which human a key belongs to — but no migration ever created the
column. On a real database every `find_by_prefix` therefore failed with
`42703 undefined column`, which is the query that authenticates every API
key. This migration closes that gap.

Security boundary: the column is nullable, because a service-account key is
owned by a service rather than by a person, and making it NOT NULL would
force every such key to borrow a human's identity. A NULL owner means "no
human behind this credential", which audit must be able to represent. It
carries no authorization weight: the key's authority is its
`tenant_id` + `organization_id` + `role` binding, resolved server-side.

It must NOT:
• be made NOT NULL — a service key legitimately has no human owner;
• be granted a foreign key that would make deleting a user delete keys;
• be used to widen a key's scope; it is attribution only.
```


**COMPLETE CONTENT** (39 lines):

```sql
-- PURPOSE: Add the owning-user column that `api_keys` projections already read.
--
-- Owning layer: the database, applied by the migration runner.
--
-- Production responsibility: create `api_keys.user_id`. The repository
-- (`crates/persistence/src/repositories/api_keys.rs`) projects `user_id` in
-- its `COLUMNS` list and reads it in `row_from`, and the API-key use-case
-- records which human a key belongs to — but no migration ever created the
-- column. On a real database every `find_by_prefix` therefore failed with
-- `42703 undefined column`, which is the query that authenticates every API
-- key. This migration closes that gap.
--
-- Security boundary: the column is nullable, because a service-account key is
-- owned by a service rather than by a person, and making it NOT NULL would
-- force every such key to borrow a human's identity. A NULL owner means "no
-- human behind this credential", which audit must be able to represent. It
-- carries no authorization weight: the key's authority is its
-- `tenant_id` + `organization_id` + `role` binding, resolved server-side.
--
-- It must NOT:
--   • be made NOT NULL — a service key legitimately has no human owner;
--   • be granted a foreign key that would make deleting a user delete keys;
--   • be used to widen a key's scope; it is attribution only.

ALTER TABLE api_keys
    ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS user_id UUID;

COMMENT ON COLUMN api_keys.user_id IS
    'Attribution only: the human the key was issued to, when there is one. '
    'NULL for service-account keys. Carries no authorization weight — a key''s '
    'authority is its tenant_id + organization_id + role binding, resolved '
    'server-side at verification time.';

-- An index for "which keys does this person hold?", the query the credential
-- management surface needs. Partial, because NULL owners are the common case
-- for service keys and indexing them would be waste.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS api_keys_user_id_idx
    ON api_keys (user_id)
    WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL;

```

## FILE: repo/enterprise-mas/rust-core/migrations/0019_scheduler_plane_role/up.sql


**PURPOSE:**

```text
The scheduler-plane database role (security Phase 14 / 25).

Owning layer: the database, applied by the migration runner.

Production responsibility: create `mas_scheduler` — the one role permitted
to scan `schedules` across every tenant — with BYPASSRLS confined to
SELECT on `schedules` and `schedule_runs`, and make it NOLOGIN until
provisioning grants it a login. `mas_app` deliberately receives no
BYPASSRLS here either.

Security boundary: the due-scan is a cross-tenant read by construction.
A scheduler replica does not serve a request; it asks "which schedules are
due anywhere?" and only learns the tenant after the row is in hand. The
exemption is therefore confined three ways — by role (never `mas_app`), by
table (`schedules` and `schedule_runs` only), and by operation (the due-scan
is SELECT; the subsequent write-back runs on `mas_app` inside a scoped
transaction for the tenant the row named).

It must NOT:
• grant BYPASSRLS to `mas_app`;
• grant `mas_scheduler` any privilege on tenant data (tasks, executions,
agents, credentials, api_keys, audit, outbox);
• make the role LOGIN (provisioning does that, deliberately).

Migration 0019 — the scheduler plane role.

WHY THIS EXISTS (security Phase 25 — worker/scheduler explicit identities)
=========================================================================
Migrations 0015 and 0017 created `mas_directory`, `mas_worker`,
`mas_outbox` and `mas_audit` for the same reason this one creates
`mas_scheduler`: a plane that cannot know its tenant before its query runs
cannot be expressed as an RLS policy, and the alternative — granting
`mas_app` BYPASSRLS — switches row-level security off for the whole
platform.

The scheduler is the one plane 0017 missed. Its tick is:

1. `list_due(now, limit)` — "which schedules are due anywhere?" The
answer spans every tenant, by definition.
2. for each due row: journal the planned tick and dispatch the run, now
that the row has told us which tenant owns it.

Step 1 is the only cross-tenant statement in the loop. Step 2 knows its
tenant and therefore runs under `mas_app` inside a scoped transaction —
the same `SET LOCAL app.current_tenant` path a request takes. Splitting the
tick this way keeps the bypass to a single SELECT on a single table instead
of letting the whole loop run exempt.

INVARIANTS
* `mas_scheduler` holds BYPASSRLS, and SELECT on exactly two tables.
* It is never the role behind a request-serving repository.
* Adding a tenant-data table must NOT widen these grants.

MIGRATION PATH (operational)
1. Apply with the migrator role.
2. Provision a credential for `mas_scheduler` in the secret manager and
grant it LOGIN. It is created NOLOGIN so an unconfigured deployment
cannot authenticate as the plane role by accident.
3. Configure `MAS_DATABASE_SCHEDULER_URL`. A deployment that leaves it
unset gets the runtime pool, whose due-scan returns zero rows under
RLS — the scheduler then idles visibly instead of silently skipping
tenants.
4. Rotation: rotate the credential, update the secret, reload.
```

## FILE: repo/enterprise-mas/rust-core/crates/scheduler-service/src/plane_store.rs


**PURPOSE:**

```text
The scheduler's schedule store: two pools, one cross-tenant read,
and a scoped transaction for everything after it.

Owning layer: `mas-scheduler-service` (the scheduler process edge).

Production responsibility: implement `mas_scheduling::store::ScheduleStorePort`
for the real database in a way that keeps row-level security in force. The
scheduler is a *plane*, not a request: it has no caller, no principal and no
tenant when its tick starts. That makes it the one component that could
justify an RLS bypass — and this module is where that justification is
confined to a single SELECT on a single table instead of being spent on the
whole tick.

Security boundary — the tick is split deliberately:

1. `list_due` runs on the **plane pool** (`mas_scheduler`). That role
holds BYPASSRLS, and its grants are `SELECT ON schedules` and
`SELECT ON schedule_runs` and nothing else (migration 0019). It cannot
read a task, an execution, an agent, a credential or an API key. The
scan is the platform's only cross-tenant read and it is the only
statement allowed to make one.
2. Every statement after the scan — `get`, `save`, `record_run` — runs on
the **runtime pool** (`mas_app`) inside
`with_authoritative_scope`, with `SET LOCAL app.current_tenant` /
`app.current_org` set from the tenant and organization the due row
itself named. The scheduler never carries a caller-supplied tenant:
the row is the authority, exactly as it is for a request.

A schedule whose tenant cannot be resolved is an error, not a scan of every
tenant. There is no fallback to the runtime pool for the due-scan: under
`mas_app` it would return zero rows, and a scheduler that silently idles is
a worse failure than one that refuses to start.

It must NOT:
• run `save`, `get` or `record_run` on the plane pool — the plane role
has no write grants, and giving it some would make the tick loop RLS-free;
• accept a tenant from configuration, an environment variable or a
completion callback; the schedule row is the only source;
• widen the due-scan limit in a way that lets one tenant's backlog starve
another's (`mas_scheduling::due` interleaves for exactly this reason).
```


**COMPLETE CONTENT** (227 lines):

```rust
//! PURPOSE: The scheduler's schedule store: two pools, one cross-tenant read,
//! and a scoped transaction for everything after it.
//!
//! Owning layer: `mas-scheduler-service` (the scheduler process edge).
//!
//! Production responsibility: implement `mas_scheduling::store::ScheduleStorePort`
//! for the real database in a way that keeps row-level security in force. The
//! scheduler is a *plane*, not a request: it has no caller, no principal and no
//! tenant when its tick starts. That makes it the one component that could
//! justify an RLS bypass — and this module is where that justification is
//! confined to a single SELECT on a single table instead of being spent on the
//! whole tick.
//!
//! Security boundary — the tick is split deliberately:
//!
//!   1. `list_due` runs on the **plane pool** (`mas_scheduler`). That role
//!      holds BYPASSRLS, and its grants are `SELECT ON schedules` and
//!      `SELECT ON schedule_runs` and nothing else (migration 0019). It cannot
//!      read a task, an execution, an agent, a credential or an API key. The
//!      scan is the platform's only cross-tenant read and it is the only
//!      statement allowed to make one.
//!   2. Every statement after the scan — `get`, `save`, `record_run` — runs on
//!      the **runtime pool** (`mas_app`) inside
//!      `with_authoritative_scope`, with `SET LOCAL app.current_tenant` /
//!      `app.current_org` set from the tenant and organization the due row
//!      itself named. The scheduler never carries a caller-supplied tenant:
//!      the row is the authority, exactly as it is for a request.
//!
//! A schedule whose tenant cannot be resolved is an error, not a scan of every
//! tenant. There is no fallback to the runtime pool for the due-scan: under
//! `mas_app` it would return zero rows, and a scheduler that silently idles is
//! a worse failure than one that refuses to start.
//!
//! It must NOT:
//!   • run `save`, `get` or `record_run` on the plane pool — the plane role
//!     has no write grants, and giving it some would make the tick loop RLS-free;
//!   • accept a tenant from configuration, an environment variable or a
//!     completion callback; the schedule row is the only source;
//!   • widen the due-scan limit in a way that lets one tenant's backlog starve
//!     another's (`mas_scheduling::due` interleaves for exactly this reason).

use mas_common::error::AppError;
use mas_common::ids::{OrganizationId, ScheduleId, TenantId};
use mas_common::result::Result;
use mas_common::timestamps::Timestamp;
use mas_domain::schedule::Schedule;
use mas_persistence::repositories::schedules::ScheduleStore;
use mas_scheduling::store::ScheduleStorePort;
use mas_security::AuthoritativeScope;
use sqlx::PgPool;
use uuid::Uuid;

use crate::squash_db;

/// The actor string recorded on scheduler-opened scopes.
///
/// It appears in audit events and in `pg_stat_activity`, so it has to say
/// which plane opened the transaction and that no human was behind it.
pub const SCHEDULER_ACTOR: &str = "service:mas-scheduler";

/// A schedule's tenancy, as the row itself states it.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct ScheduleTenancy {
    tenant_id: TenantId,
    organization_id: OrganizationId,
}

impl ScheduleTenancy {
    /// The authoritative scope for work on this schedule.
    fn scope(self) -> AuthoritativeScope {
        AuthoritativeScope::resolved(self.tenant_id, self.organization_id, SCHEDULER_ACTOR)
    }
}

/// The scheduler's schedule store: plane pool for the scan, runtime pool for
/// the scoped work the scan leads to.
#[derive(Debug)]
pub struct SchedulerPlaneStore {
    /// `mas_scheduler` — cross-tenant due-scan, SELECT on two tables.
    plane: PgPool,
    /// `mas_app` — every write, inside a tenant-scoped transaction.
    runtime: PgPool,
}

impl SchedulerPlaneStore {
    /// Binds the store to the two pools the tick needs.
    #[must_use]
    pub fn new(plane: PgPool, runtime: PgPool) -> Self {
        Self { plane, runtime }
    }

    /// Reads a schedule's tenancy from the row.
    ///
    /// This is the one pre-scope read in the tick, and it is the reason the
    /// plane role exists: there is no scope yet, so no RLS policy can admit
    /// the read. It returns the row's own tenant and organization — never a
    /// value from configuration or from the caller.
    ///
    /// # Errors
    /// `not_found` when the schedule does not exist; the mapped database error
    /// otherwise.
    async fn tenancy_of(&self, schedule_id: ScheduleId) -> Result<ScheduleTenancy> {
        let row: Option<(Uuid, Uuid)> =
            sqlx::query_as("SELECT tenant_id, organization_id FROM schedules WHERE id = $1")
                .bind(Uuid::from(schedule_id))
                .fetch_optional(&self.plane)
                .await
                .map_err(squash_db)?;
        let (tenant, organization) =
            row.ok_or_else(|| AppError::not_found("schedule", schedule_id.to_string()))?;
        Ok(ScheduleTenancy {
            tenant_id: TenantId::from_uuid(tenant),
            organization_id: OrganizationId::from_uuid(organization),
        })
    }

    /// Runs `work` on the runtime pool inside the schedule's own scope.
    ///
    /// The scope comes from the schedule row, so a scheduler replica cannot be
    /// steered at another tenant's data by anything the network hands it. The
    /// closure runs inside one transaction: a failed write-back rolls back
    /// with the rest of the tick's work rather than half-applying.
    async fn in_schedule_scope<T, F, Fut>(&self, tenancy: ScheduleTenancy, work: F) -> Result<T>
    where
        F: FnOnce() -> Fut,
        Fut: core::future::Future<Output = Result<T>>,
    {
        mas_persistence::scoped_request::with_authoritative_scope(
            &self.runtime,
            tenancy.scope(),
            work,
        )
        .await
    }
}

#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl ScheduleStorePort for SchedulerPlaneStore {
    /// The cross-tenant due-scan.
    ///
    /// Runs on the plane connection. Under any other role this returns zero
    /// rows rather than every tenant's schedules, which is the correct
    /// direction for the failure to go: a misconfigured scheduler idles
    /// visibly instead of leaking tenancy.
    async fn list_due(&self, now: &Timestamp, limit: usize) -> Result<Vec<Schedule>> {
        let mut connection = self.plane.acquire().await.map_err(squash_db)?;
        ScheduleStore::list_due_in(connection.as_mut(), now, limit).await
    }

    /// Loads one schedule: resolve the tenancy on the plane, then read the row
    /// under that tenant's scope.
    ///
    /// A schedule id belonging to another tenant resolves to a scope that
    /// cannot see it, so the answer is `None` — indistinguishable from "does
    /// not exist", which is what an unauthorized id must look like.
    async fn get(&self, id: ScheduleId) -> Result<Option<Schedule>> {
        let tenancy = self.tenancy_of(id).await?;
        self.in_schedule_scope(tenancy, || async move {
            let mut connection = mas_persistence::scoped_request::connection().await?;
            ScheduleStore::get_in(connection.connection().as_mut(), id).await
        })
        .await
    }

    /// Persists the post-fire schedule state: same schedule, same tenant, and
    /// the write runs inside that tenant's scoped transaction.
    async fn save(&self, schedule: &Schedule) -> Result<()> {
        let tenancy = ScheduleTenancy {
            tenant_id: schedule.tenant_id,
            // The domain aggregate is tenant-scoped by design and does not
            // carry the organization; the row does, and the row is the
            // authority. Reading it here keeps the scope honest without
            // widening the aggregate's contract.
            organization_id: self.tenancy_of(schedule.id).await?.organization_id,
        };
        let stored = schedule.clone();
        self.in_schedule_scope(tenancy, move || async move {
            let mut connection = mas_persistence::scoped_request::connection().await?;
            ScheduleStore::save_in(connection.connection().as_mut(), &stored).await
        })
        .await
    }

    /// Journals a planned tick under the schedule's own scope.
    ///
    /// `false` means another replica recorded this tick first — the
    /// duplicate-fire guard. The unique constraint is what actually decides;
    /// this only reports the outcome.
    async fn record_run(&self, schedule_id: ScheduleId, planned_at: Timestamp) -> Result<bool> {
        let tenancy = self.tenancy_of(schedule_id).await?;
        self.in_schedule_scope(tenancy, move || async move {
            let mut connection = mas_persistence::scoped_request::connection().await?;
            ScheduleStore::record_run_in(connection.connection().as_mut(), schedule_id, planned_at)
                .await
        })
        .await
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    /// The actor string must name the plane, because it is what an auditor
    /// reads in `audit_events.actor` when a tick is questioned.
    #[test]
    fn the_actor_string_names_the_plane() {
        assert!(SCHEDULER_ACTOR.contains("mas-scheduler"));
        assert!(SCHEDULER_ACTOR.starts_with("service:"));
    }

    /// The scope a tenancy produces must carry the row's own ids — not a
    /// default, not a nil, not something the caller supplied.
    #[test]
    fn a_tenancy_produces_a_scope_from_the_row() {
        let tenant = TenantId::new();
        let organization = OrganizationId::new();
        let scope = ScheduleTenancy {
            tenant_id: tenant,
            organization_id: organization,
        }
        .scope();
        assert_eq!(scope.tenant_id(), tenant);
        assert_eq!(scope.organization_id(), organization);
        assert!(scope.actor().contains("mas-scheduler"));
    }
}

```

## FILE: python-orchestrator/tests/bridge/test_internal_signature.py


**PURPOSE:**

```text
Tests that the bridge verifies the body-bound, time-bounded signature on
every inbound internal call, and that the verification is a real check and
not a header presence test.

Covers spec §9 and §10: internal service authentication. Being able to reach
the port is not an identity, and holding a bearer token is not proof that
*this* message was sent by its holder. Only an HMAC over the exact request
bytes, bound to the calling service and to the moment it was made, establishes
that. Every rejection must be indistinguishable from every other, so the
response is not an oracle for which check failed.
```


**COMPLETE CONTENT** (267 lines):

```python
# PURPOSE:
# Tests that the bridge verifies the body-bound, time-bounded signature on
# every inbound internal call, and that the verification is a real check and
# not a header presence test.
#
# Covers spec §9 and §10: internal service authentication. Being able to reach
# the port is not an identity, and holding a bearer token is not proof that
# *this* message was sent by its holder. Only an HMAC over the exact request
# bytes, bound to the calling service and to the moment it was made, establishes
# that. Every rejection must be indistinguishable from every other, so the
# response is not an oracle for which check failed.

"""Body-bound internal signature tests for the Rust -> Python bridge.

The threat these tests encode is a caller that holds (or has captured) a valid
bearer credential and can therefore reach the port, but is not the service it
claims to be — or is replaying a call it captured earlier, or has altered the
body in flight.

Four variants matter and are tested separately:

* **Unsigned** — a valid credential and no signature. Refused: a configured
  secret makes the signature mandatory.
* **Tampered** — a valid signature over a *different* body. Refused: a
  signature over one request is not a signature over another.
* **Unknown service** — a syntactically perfect signature from a service that
  is not on the allowlist. Refused.
* **Stale** — a valid signature whose timestamp is outside the skew window.
  Refused: this is the replay defence.

The positive case is tested too, because a verification that refuses
everything is not a working control — it is an outage.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import grpc
import pytest
from tests.bridge.conftest import (
    INTERNAL_SERVICE,
    SIGNING_SECRET,
    BridgeHarness,
    internal_signature_pairs,
    metadata,
    request,
)

from mas_orchestrator.grpc.errors import is_retryable_status
from mas_orchestrator.security.internal_service import (
    MAX_SKEW_SECONDS,
    now_millis,
)

pytestmark = pytest.mark.asyncio(loop_scope="function")


async def _run(
    harness: BridgeHarness,
    message=None,
    extra_pairs: list[tuple[str, str]] | None = None,
):
    """Calls ``RunAgent`` with the given metadata appended to the standard set.

    Args:
        harness: The running bridge.
        message: The request to send. Built fresh when omitted.
        extra_pairs: Additional metadata pairs (typically the signature).

    Returns:
        The reply.

    Raises:
        grpc.aio.AioRpcError: When the call is aborted.
    """
    message = message if message is not None else request()
    pairs = metadata(tenant_id=message.tenant_id, organization_id=message.organization_id) + list(
        extra_pairs or ()
    )
    stub, channel = harness.stub()
    try:
        return await stub.RunAgent(message, metadata=pairs)
    finally:
        await channel.close()


class TestSignedCallIsAccepted:
    """A correctly signed call must reach the runtime."""

    async def test_a_signed_call_dispatches(self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness) -> None:
        """A valid signature over the exact body is accepted and dispatched."""
        message = request()
        await _run(signed_bridge, message, internal_signature_pairs(message))

        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 1

    async def test_an_unsigned_bridge_still_accepts_unsigned_calls(
        self, bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """With no secret configured the check is skipped, not failed.

        This is the development posture. It is asserted explicitly so a change
        that accidentally makes an unprovisioned bridge refuse all traffic is
        caught here rather than in an environment.
        """
        await _run(bridge, request(), None)

        assert bridge.service.call_count == 1


class TestUnsignedCallIsRefused:
    """A configured secret makes the signature mandatory."""

    async def test_a_valid_credential_without_a_signature_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """The bearer token alone is not enough once signing is configured."""
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, request(), None)

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0

    async def test_a_refused_signature_is_never_retryable(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """Authentication failures are permanent; retrying them is an outage."""
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, request(), None)

        assert is_retryable_status(raised.value) is False


class TestTamperedBodyIsRefused:
    """A signature over one message is not a signature over another."""

    async def test_a_signature_over_a_different_body_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """Sign one request, send another: the MAC cannot match."""
        signed_for = request(input_json="hello")
        sent = request(input_json="hello but different")

        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, sent, internal_signature_pairs(signed_for))

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0

    async def test_a_signature_over_a_different_tenant_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """Retargeting a captured call at another tenant fails the MAC.

        This is the cross-tenant case for the bridge: an attacker who captures
        tenant A's signed call cannot replay it against tenant B, because the
        tenant is inside the signed bytes.
        """
        signed_for = request(tenant_id="tenant-alpha")
        retargeted = request(tenant_id="tenant-beta")

        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, retargeted, internal_signature_pairs(signed_for))

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0

    async def test_a_signature_over_a_different_service_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """Signing as an unpermitted service is refused even with the right key."""
        message = request()
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(
                signed_bridge,
                message,
                internal_signature_pairs(message, service="mas-attacker"),
            )

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0


class TestStaleSignatureIsRefused:
    """The timestamp bound is the replay defence."""

    async def test_a_signature_outside_the_skew_window_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """A captured call replayed an hour later does not verify."""
        message = request()
        stale = now_millis() - (MAX_SKEW_SECONDS * 1000) - 60_000
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, message, internal_signature_pairs(message, at_ms=stale))

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0

    async def test_a_signature_from_the_future_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """Skew is measured in both directions, not only backwards."""
        message = request()
        future = now_millis() + (MAX_SKEW_SECONDS * 1000) + 60_000
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(signed_bridge, message, internal_signature_pairs(message, at_ms=future))

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0


class TestWrongSecretIsRefused:
    """A signature under a different secret proves nothing."""

    async def test_a_signature_under_another_secret_is_refused(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """The MAC is keyed; a correct structure with the wrong key fails."""
        message = request()
        with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
            await _run(
                signed_bridge,
                message,
                internal_signature_pairs(message, secret="not-the-secret"),
            )

        assert raised.value.code() is grpc.StatusCode.UNAUTHENTICATED
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0

    async def test_every_refusal_is_indistinguishable(self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness) -> None:
        """No failure mode may be told apart from another by its message.

        If "wrong key" and "stale timestamp" produced different responses, the
        bridge would be an oracle that lets a prober confirm which secret it
        guessed correctly.
        """
        message = request()
        messages = []

        variants: list[list[tuple[str, str]] | None] = [
            None,
            internal_signature_pairs(request(input_json="other")),
            internal_signature_pairs(message, secret="not-the-secret"),
            internal_signature_pairs(message, service="mas-attacker"),
            internal_signature_pairs(message, at_ms=now_millis() - 600_000),
        ]
        for pairs in variants:
            with pytest.raises(grpc.aio.AioRpcError) as raised:
                await _run(signed_bridge, message, pairs)
            messages.append(raised.value.details())

        assert len(set(messages)) == 1, f"refusals differ: {messages}"
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 0


class TestServiceAllowlist:
    """The allowlist is enforced even for a cryptographically valid signature."""

    async def test_the_configured_worker_service_is_accepted(
        self, signed_bridge: BridgeHarness
    ) -> None:
        """The id the Rust worker presents is on the default allowlist."""
        message = request()
        await _run(signed_bridge, message, internal_signature_pairs(message))

        assert INTERNAL_SERVICE == "mas-worker"
        assert SIGNING_SECRET
        assert signed_bridge.service.call_count == 1

```

## FILE: repo/enterprise-mas/rust-core/crates/persistence/src/durable.rs


**PURPOSE:**

```text
The production implementation of [`DurableExecutionPort`] — the one place
where the canonical execution pipeline touches the database.

Every method here is exactly one transaction. That is the whole point of
the port: the caller cannot create an execution without its task, its
attempt, its audit row and its outbox rows, because there is no API that
writes only some of them.

Security boundary — which transaction that is depends on the caller, and
getting it wrong silently disables row-level security:

* **Inside a request** (HTTP, gRPC) the operation *joins* the transaction
the middleware already opened, in which `app.current_tenant` is armed. It
does not open a second connection: a second connection has no GUC, and
under `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` a connection with no GUC reads and
writes nothing. Opening one here would both drop the scope and split one
request's writes across two transactions.
* **On the worker / outbox plane** there is no request and no tenant in
advance — the plane's tenant authority is the row it wins a lease on.
Those callers open and commit their own transaction, and must connect as
`mas_worker` / `mas_outbox`, whose `BYPASSRLS` is confined by table and
operation. They must never connect as `mas_app`.

Layer / ownership
-----------------
`mas-persistence`. It owns SQL; `mas-application` owns the vocabulary and
the decision-making. Nothing above this file knows a table name.

Production responsibility
-------------------------
* **Atomic submission** — idempotency, execution, task, attempt, audit and
outbox commit together or not at all. Nothing is reported successful
before the commit succeeds.
* **DB-enforced idempotency** — the partial unique index on
`(tenant_id, idempotency_key)` decides who won. There is no
SELECT-then-INSERT here, because a SELECT-then-INSERT races.
* **Real durable claims** — `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside the same
transaction that writes the attempt row and installs the ownership
fence. Two workers cannot both claim one task, because the row lock and
the partial unique index on open attempts both forbid it.
* **Stale-write rejection** — every settlement carries the version the
caller observed; an `UPDATE ... WHERE version = $expected` that matches
no row is a lost ownership race and is reported as `Conflict`, never as
success.
* **Terminal state before ack** — `settle` commits and only then returns.
The caller acks the broker afterwards.

What this module must NOT do
----------------------------
* It must NOT open a second connection or a second transaction inside a
unit: every write goes through the one `&mut PgConnection` the unit owns.
* It must NOT mark work published/completed before the durable write
commits.
* It must NOT derive attempt counts from broker delivery metadata — the
attempt number comes from `task_attempts` and from nowhere else.
* It must NOT log row payloads: task inputs and results may contain
secrets. Only ids, statuses and codes are logged.
```


**COMPLETE CONTENT** (1982 lines):

//! What this module must NOT do
//! ----------------------------
//! * It must NOT open a second connection or a second transaction inside a
//!   unit: every write goes through the one `&mut PgConnection` the unit owns.
//! * It must NOT mark work published/completed before the durable write
//!   commits.
//! * It must NOT derive attempt counts from broker delivery metadata — the
//!   attempt number comes from `task_attempts` and from nowhere else.
//! * It must NOT log row payloads: task inputs and results may contain
//!   secrets. Only ids, statuses and codes are logged.

    CancellationReceipt, CancellationRequest, CancellationResult, ClaimQuery, DurableExecutionPort,
    ExecutionAction, ExecutionOutcome, ExecutionTransitionReceipt, ExecutionTransitionRequest,
    ExecutionUsage, PipelineCounters, SettlementReceipt, SubmissionIntent, SubmissionKind,
    SubmissionReceipt, TaskClaim, TaskOutcome, TaskSettlement, UsageObservation,
};

use mas_domain::{
    ActorKind, ActorRef, AttemptStatus, AuditActor, AuditActorKind, AuditEvent, AuditOutcome,
    CancellationOutcome, Execution, StateTransition, Task, TaskAttempt, TransitionActor,
    UsageRecord,
};
